'''''Heliotropium curassavicum''''', commonly called '''salt heliotrope''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Heliotropiaceae]]. It is native to the [[Americas]] and Northern Australia (<ref>https://florabase.dbca.wa.gov.au/browse/profile/6707</ref><ref>https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/scotia/key/Plants%20and%20Fungi%20of%20south%20western%20NSW/Media/Html/Heliotropium_curassavicum.htm</ref> has been introduced elsewhere.

==Description==
''Heliotropium curassavicum'' is a [[perennial]] herb which can take the form of a prostrate [[Vine|creeper]] along the ground to a somewhat erect [[shrub]] approaching {{convert|0.5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in height. The stem and foliage are fleshy, with the leaves thick and oval or spade-shaped.

The plentiful [[inflorescence]]s are curled, coiling double rows of small bell-shaped [[flower]]s. Each flower is white with five rounded lobes and a purple or yellow throat. The [[fruit]] is a smooth nutlet.

==Taxonomy==
There are five currently recognized varieties.<ref name="Al-Shehbaz">{{cite journal |last1=Al-Shehbaz |first1=Ihsan |date=1991 |title=The genera of Boraginaceae in the southeastern United States |journal=Journal of the Arnold Arboretum. Supplementary Series |volume=1 |pages=1–169 |jstor=43782784}}</ref> These are:
*''H. curassavicum'' var. ''argentinum'' - Native to the tropics of [[South America]], including [[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], [[Paraguay]], and [[Uruguay]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnston |first1=Ivan |date=1928 |title=Studies in the Boraginaceae |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/39600182#page/15/mode/1up |journal= Contributions from the Gray Herbarium of Harvard University |volume=81 |pages=15 |access-date=2 February 2018 }}</ref> 
*''H. curassavicum'' var. ''curassavicum'' - Globally widespread, native from the eastern U.S. to Argentina, and naturalized on seashores elsewhere.<ref name=Al-Shehbaz/> It has the smallest flowers, being only 2.5–3.5 mm wide
*''H. curassavicum'' var. ''fruticulosum'' - Endemic to the [[San Juan Province, Argentina|San Juan]] and [[Mendoza, Argentina|Mendoza]] provinces of Argentina.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnston |first1=Ivan |date=1959 |title=Some noteworthy American borages |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/765970#page/21/mode/1up |journal=Wrightia  |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=15 |access-date=2 February 2018 }}</ref>
*''H. curassavicum'' var. ''obovatum'' - Widespread in western North America and [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua, Mexico]].<ref name=AZ>{{cite book |last1=Kearney |first1=Thomas |last2=Peebles |first2=Robert |date=1942 |title=Flowering plants and ferns of Arizona |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/132362 |publisher=[[U.S. Dept. of Agriculture]] |page=743 }}</ref> Its flowers are 5–10 mm wide, with yellow or slightly purple-tinged throats.
*''H. curassavicum'' var. ''oculatum'' - Native from southwestern Utah to [[Baja California]].<ref name=AZ/> Its flowers are 3–5 mm wide with purple throats.

== Distribution and habitat ==
The species is native to Northern Australia including the Northern Territory, Western Australia and Queensland, and to much of the [[Americas]], from [[Canada]] to [[Argentina]], including the [[West Indies]] and Hawaii. It can be found as an [[introduced species]] (in some cases being [[Invasive species|invasive]]) in Africa, Eurasia, and southern Australia.<ref name="Al-Shehbaz" />

It thrives in [[Halophyte|salty]] soils, such as beach sand, [[Dry lake|alkali flats]], and salt marshes.<ref name="Al-Shehbaz" /> It is often found in disturbed coastal sites.<ref>[http://www.regionalconservation.org/beta/nfyn/plantdetail.asp?tx=Helicura Seaside heliotrope] The Institute for Regional Conservation</ref>

== Common names ==
Due to its wide geographical range that spans many nations and languages, ''H. curassavicum'' has been given an assortment of common names. In English, these include salt heliotrope,<ref>{{PLANTS|id=hecu3|taxon=Heliotropium curassavicum|accessdate=2 February 2018}}</ref> seaside heliotrope, monkey tail, quail plant and Chinese parsley. In [[Latin American Spanish]], it is known as {{lang|es|cola de mico}}, {{lang|es|cola de gama}} or {{lang|es|rabo alacrán}}. It is called {{lang|haw|kīpūkai}} in [[Hawaiian language|Hawaii]].{{Citation needed|date=October 2025}}
